questions.stem: What does the theoretical ionic model assume about the ions?

options.text: Perfectly spherical ions with purely electrostatic attractions
options.explanation: The ideal model allows no distortion and no sharing.

options.text: Partially shared electron pairs between the ions
options.explanation: Sharing is the covalent contamination the model excludes.

options.text: Diffuse electron clouds that overlap freely
options.explanation: Overlap signals covalent character, absent from the ideal.

options.text: Ions of changing charge with temperature
options.explanation: Charges are fixed whole values in the model.

questions.stem: Why can measured lattice energy differ from the theoretical value?

options.text: The theoretical formula forgot a constant
options.explanation: The formula is fine; the ionic assumption is what fails.

options.text: Polarisation of the anion adds covalent character the model omits
options.explanation: Distorted electron density means the pure electrostatic bookkeeping misses energy.

options.text: Instruments cannot read lattice energies accurately
options.explanation: The gap is chemical, not instrumental.
The discrepancy arises from bonding character, not size drift.

questions.stem: During polarisation, which species pulls on which electrons?

options.explanation: No further exchange happens; one side deforms.
Polarisation is precisely that mutual electrical influence.

options.text: The cation attracts electrons from the anion
options.explanation: The positive ion distorts the negative ion's electron density toward itself.

options.text: The anion attracts electrons from the cation
options.explanation: The distortion runs the other way; anions are the polarised party.

questions.stem: What is the electron-level signature of covalent character creeping into an ionic bond?

options.explanation: Spherical ions are the pure ionic picture, not the covalent contamination.

options.text: The ionic charges become fractional in the model
options.explanation: The model keeps whole charges; reality deforms density instead.

options.text: The electrons transfer completely to the cation
options.explanation: Full transfer is the ionic ideal, not partial sharing.

options.text: The anion's electron density is distorted toward the region between the ions
options.explanation: Shared-ish density between the nuclei is the covalent hallmark.

questions.stem: A compound shows a measured lattice energy noticeably below its theoretical value. The best explanation is

options.text: significant polarisation of the anion has introduced covalent character
options.explanation: Distorted, partly shared density releases extra stabilisation the ionic model cannot price.
Defects are a different story; the model gap here points at bonding character.
Perfect spheres would close the gap, not open it.
Full ionic character would match the theoretical value.

questions.stem: State the two assumptions of the perfect ionic model that polarisation breaks.
questions.modelAnswer: Ions are 100% spherical and the attractions between them are purely electrostatic.
Polarisation is the distortion of an anion's electron density by the cation's attraction, which introduces covalent character into the ionic bond.

questions.stem: Explain why anion polarisation pushes the measured lattice energy away from the theoretical prediction.
questions.modelAnswer: The theoretical number prices purely electrostatic attraction between undistorted spheres; once the cation draws anion electron density inward, the bond carries partial covalent character and its true energy departs from the ionic-only calculation.

questions.stem: A compound of a small, doubly charged cation and a huge anion shows a large theoretical-to-measured lattice energy gap. Assemble the causal chain.
questions.modelAnswer: The small, highly charged cation has strong polarising power, the huge anion is easily distorted, so substantial electron density shifts toward the cation, covalent character grows, and the measured lattice energy falls well below the perfect-ionic calculation.

questions.stem: Which quantity measures a cation's polarising ability?

options.explanation: Mass does not enter the electrostatic distortion.

options.text: Charge density - charge over surface area
options.explanation: Concentrated charge distorts anions hardest.
Electrons belong to the anion side of the story.
Neutrons carry no charge and no pull.

questions.stem: Why does K+ polarise less strongly than Li+?

options.explanation: Potassium has more protons; density still falls.
Lithium forms the cation here.

options.text: K+ has a greater ionic radius, spreading the same charge over more area
options.explanation: Charge density falls as the ion swells.
Both are 1+ ions; size is the difference.

questions.stem: Why does Mg2+ carry more polarising power than Na+?

options.explanation: Mg2+ is not larger; its charge is the argument.
Neutrons play no role.

options.text: It is an anion with extra electrons
options.explanation: Mg2+ is the cation that lost electrons.

options.text: Its charge is larger, doubling the density on a similar-sized ion
options.explanation: 2+ against 1+ at comparable radius wins the density contest.

questions.stem: Which anion is the more polarisable, and why?

options.text: Br- - its larger ionic radius makes its electron cloud easier to distort
options.explanation: Bigger clouds are more easily squashed.

options.text: Cl- - its smaller radius concentrates its electrons
options.explanation: Concentration aids resistance, not distortion.
Both carry a single negative charge.
Mass is not the mechanism; radius is.

questions.stem: The greatest polarising power belongs to a cation that is

options.explanation: The weakest combination of the four.
Both properties concentrate charge density.
Size dilutes the density even at high charge.
Low charge caps the density however small the ion.

questions.stem: State how charge density is calculated for a cation.
questions.modelAnswer: Charge density is the charge of the cation divided by its surface area.

questions.stem: State the relative polarisability of Br- and Cl- with the reason.
questions.modelAnswer: Br- is more polarisable than Cl- because its ionic radius is larger, so its electron cloud distorts more easily.

questions.stem: Explain why small, highly charged cations dominate the polarising-power ranking.
questions.modelAnswer: Charge density - charge per unit surface area - is the measure of the cation's field at the anion; shrinking the radius or multiplying the charge concentrates that field, and the two effects compound in the same direction.

questions.stem: Rank Li+, K+, Mg2+ and Ba2+ by polarising power and justify each step.
questions.modelAnswer: Mg2+ and Li+ top the list for their high charge density - Mg2+ for its doubled charge, Li+ for its tiny radius; Na+ follows behind Mg2+ on charge; K+ and the even larger Ba2+ trail, their spread-out charge diluting the density.
